lines: Your shop did 500 tune-ups at 40 dollars: 20,000 dollars of sales. The income statement shows how much of that was profit, from the top line down to the bottom line.
Start with revenue: 20,000 dollars. Subtract the cost of goods sold, the parts, 5,000 dollars. That leaves 15,000 dollars of gross profit, a 75 percent gross margin.
Next, operating expenses: the cost of running the place. Rent, insurance and ads add up to 11,400 dollars. Plus depreciation: a 3,000 dollar tool kit that lasts 5 years counts as 600 dollars a year.
Gross profit minus 12,000 dollars of operating expenses is 3,000 dollars of operating income, also called EBIT, earnings before interest and taxes. That's a 15 percent operating margin.
Then subtract interest, 200 dollars, and taxes. Your LLC is pass-through, so taxes here are zero. Paying back loan principal isn't an expense; only the interest is.
Net income, the bottom line, is 2,800 dollars: a 14 percent net margin. As a C corporation, a 21 percent tax would leave 2,212 dollars.
Like a tree that burns much of its energy just to stay alive, a business can bring in a lot and keep a little. Always read down to the net.
